lead: A computer cannot reason over English words directly. It needs a sentence's meaning written in a formal language with exact syntax and exact semantics. Such a language is a meaning representation, and first-order logic is the standard one. Each sentence maps to a logical form. Inference is now a search over those forms rather than over English. In full FOL that search is not guaranteed to halt, which is why deployed systems use restricted languages where it does. The same machinery drives question answering over databases and ontology reasoners.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 on levels of language analysis; Unit 3 on syntax trees helps but is not required.

sections.h3: What a meaning representation must do

blocks.text: A sentence is only a string of words until its meaning is stored in a form a machine can compute with. That form is a meaning representation (MR): a formal language with fixed syntax and fixed semantics. Semantic analysis maps each sentence to one expression of it, the sentence's logical form. Inference works on logical forms, never on English.

items: Verifiability: decide against a database whether the expression is true or false.
Unambiguity: one expression, one reading; word-sense and attachment ambiguity settled before mapping.

Canonical form: sentences that mean the same get the same form. 'Gita sold the car to Ravi' and 'Ravi bought the car from Gita' should map to one predicate with the same argument slots, say Sell(Gita, car, Ravi), possibly linked by meaning postulates between buy and sell. The equivalence comes from that shared form, not from the connectives.
Inferencing: new expressions follow from old ones, so questions never stored can still be answered.
Expressiveness: can state every, some, negation, time without losing distinctions.

blocks.text: The requirements pull against each other. A richer language says more but makes inference slower; a poorer one is fast but cannot express 'every' or 'some'. First-order logic (FOL) is the usual compromise, and most semantic parsers output it or a close variant.

FOL builds expressions from a small vocabulary. Constants name fixed individuals: Ravi, book1, chennai. Variables are placeholders: x, y, e. A function takes terms and returns a term, as in FatherOf(Ravi). Constants, variables and function applications are terms; a term denotes an object, never a truth value.

Predicates take terms and return a truth value: Student(Ravi), Reads(Ravi, book1). A predicate applied to the right number of terms is an atomic formula. Atomic formulae combine with the connectives ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (implies) and ↔ (if and only if), with brackets fixing grouping.

Quantifiers bind variables. ∀x means 'for every object x in the domain'; ∃x means 'there is at least one'. The formula a quantifier attaches to is its scope. An occurrence inside its own quantifier's scope is bound, otherwise free. In ∀x(Student(x) → Reads(x, y)) the x is bound and the y is free. A formula with a free variable is not a sentence: it is true or false only once each free variable is given a value by a variable assignment; without an assignment it has no truth value. A formula with no free variables is closed, or a sentence.

Syntax alone is empty; meaning comes from a model M = (D, F). D is the non-empty domain of objects. F is the interpretation function: it sends each constant to one element of D, each n-ary predicate to a set of n-tuples from D, and each function symbol to a mapping from n-tuples to elements.

Take D = {Ravi, Meera, book1}, with F(Student) = {Ravi, Meera} and F(Reads) = {(Ravi, book1), (Meera, book1)}. Reads is a set of 2-tuples. An atomic formula is true exactly when its argument tuple lies in the relation.

M satisfies φ, written M ⊨ φ, when φ comes out true under F. Entailment: KB ⊨ φ when every model that satisfies the knowledge base KB also satisfies φ. That is the formal 'φ follows from what we know'. The direction matters — KB ⊨ φ does not give φ ⊨ KB. A formula true in every model is valid; one true in at least one model is satisfiable.

sections.h3: Restricted quantifiers, events and description logics

blocks.text: English quantifiers are restricted. 'Every student reads a book' quantifies over students, not over everything. Write the restriction with →:

blocks.where: Student(x) means x is a student; Book(y) means y is a book; Reads(x, y) means x reads y; → is implication and ∧ is conjunction.

blocks.text: Inside ∀ use →; inside ∃ use ∧. Writing ∀x(Student(x) ∧ Reads(x, book1)) says every object in the whole domain is a student who reads book1. Writing ∃y(Book(y) → Reads(Ravi, y)) is nearly always true, because any non-book satisfies it for free.

Verbs need arguments beyond their surface ones. Davidson's event representation adds a hidden event variable. In Davidson's original form the verb keeps its own arguments: 'Meera read a book in the library on Monday' becomes ∃e(Read(e, Meera, book1) ∧ Place(e, library) ∧ Time(e, Monday)). A fully separated variant, the neo-Davidsonian style, splits them into Reader(e, Meera) and Object(e, book1). Either way each modifier is a separate conjunct, so adding 'slowly' adds Slowly(e) without changing any predicate's arity. This is the bridge to semantic roles, see 4.6.

Description logics (DL) are decidable fragments of FOL used for ontologies. They split the vocabulary into concepts (classes, like unary predicates) and roles (binary relations). Schema statements go in the TBox; facts about individuals go in the ABox. The key inference is subsumption: Student ⊑ ∃reads.Book says every student reads at least one book, and a reasoner checks whether one concept is subsumed by another. Only a few syllabi teach this in detail; know the vocabulary and this example.

spec.aria: Two models side by side: Ravi, Meera and Gita on the left, book1 and book2 on the right. In the first, Reads arrows go from Ravi to book1 and Meera to book2 and the formula is true; in the second only Ravi has an arrow and the formula is false.

examples.question: Represent 'Every student reads a book' in first-order logic. Domain D = {Ravi, Meera, Gita, book1, book2}. Student = {Ravi, Meera}; Book = {book1, book2}; Reads = {(Ravi, book1), (Meera, book2)}. (a) Write the formula. (b) Show that the model satisfies it. (c) Change Reads to {(Ravi, book1)} and say why the formula is false. (d) Explain why ∃y(Book(y) ∧ ∀x(Student(x) → Reads(x,y))) entails the original formula but the original does not entail it.
steps: (b) x = Ravi: Student(Ravi) true, so find y. y = book1: Book(book1) true and (Ravi, book1) ∈ Reads. Satisfied. x = Meera: y = book2 works. x = Gita, book1, book2: Student false, so each implication is true with no obligation. 2 of 2 students have a book, so M ⊨ formula.

(c) Reads = {(Ravi, book1)}: x = Ravi still holds. For x = Meera, Student(Meera) is true but no y gives Book(y) ∧ Reads(Meera, y), so that implication is false and the ∀ fails. 1 of 2 students has a book.

(d) The swapped form needs one book read by every student: 0 books qualify here. But if some book b is read by all students, every student reads b, so the original holds. Hence the swapped form entails the original, and not the reverse.
examples.answer: ∀x(Student(x) → ∃y(Book(y) ∧ Reads(x,y))); true in the model because 2 of 2 students have a book, false when Reads = {(Ravi, book1)} because only 1 of 2 does, and the swapped form is strictly stronger since 0 books are read by every student.

traps: ∀ pairs with → and ∃ pairs with ∧. ∀x(Student(x) ∧ Reads(x, book1)) forces every object in the domain to be a student.
∀x∃y is not ∃y∀x. The first lets the book depend on the student; the second demands one book for everybody.
A formula with a free variable is not a sentence. Without a variable assignment it has no truth value.
KB ⊨ φ is not φ ⊨ KB. Entailment runs from the knowledge base to the query.
True in one model is not valid. Valid means true in every model; satisfiable means true in at least one.

quiz.q: State the canonical form requirement for a meaning representation.
quiz.a: Sentences with the same meaning map to the same, or logically equivalent, logical forms, so one stored form serves all paraphrases.

quiz.q: Why is → used with ∀ but ∧ with ∃ in restricted quantification?
quiz.a: ∀x(Student(x) → P(x)) is automatically true for non-students, since a false antecedent makes the implication true, so only students are constrained. ∃x(Student(x) ∧ P(x)) needs one object that is both; with → a non-student would satisfy it.

quiz.q: Domain D = {Ravi, Meera, book1}, Student = {Ravi, Meera}, Book = {book1}, Reads = {(Ravi, book1)}. Is ∀x(Student(x) → ∃y(Book(y) ∧ Reads(x,y))) true?
quiz.a: False. x = Ravi is satisfied with y = book1. x = Meera: Student(Meera) true but no y gives Book(y) ∧ Reads(Meera, y), so that implication is false and the ∀ fails.

quiz.q: Using the chapter's model, compare ∀x∃y and ∃y∀x for the reading formula.
quiz.a: ∀x(Student(x) → ∃y(Book(y) ∧ Reads(x,y))) is true: Ravi reads book1, Meera book2. ∃y(Book(y) ∧ ∀x(Student(x) → Reads(x,y))) is false: 0 books are read by both. The second entails the first, not the reverse.

quiz.q: Distinguish free and bound occurrences of a variable.
quiz.a: An occurrence inside the scope of a quantifier on that variable is bound; otherwise free. In ∀x(Student(x) → Reads(x, y)) the x is bound and y is free, so the formula is not closed.

quiz.q: A formula is true in the model of the worked example. Does that make it valid?
quiz.a: No. True in one model means satisfiable. Valid means true in every model, e.g. ∀x(Student(x) ∨ ¬Student(x)). Validity is entailment from an empty knowledge base.

quiz.q: Give a Davidson event representation of 'Ravi read a book in Chennai on Monday'.
quiz.a: ∃e(Read(e, Ravi, book1) ∧ Place(e, Chennai) ∧ Time(e, Monday)). The event variable e carries every modifier as its own conjunct, so no predicate changes arity.

beyond: Not for the exam. Description logics underlie OWL ontologies; reasoners checking Student ⊑ ∃reads.Book run inside biomedical knowledge graphs and product catalogues. Event representations feed semantic-role labeling (4.6) and frames (4.4). Semantic parsers over databases emit a logical form and execute it — verifiability in production. Search 'description logic EL++', 'Davidsonian events', 'natural logic' to go further.
